o: The justice and power of the Lord.
bg: nahum, book of

Nahum prophesied, according to some, in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz (B.C. 743). Others, however, think that his prophecies are to be referred to the latter half of the reign of Hezekiah (about B.C. 709).
Nineveh

First mentioned in Gen. 10:11, which is rendered in the Revised Version, "He [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria and builded Nineveh." It is not again noticed till the days of Jonah, when it is described (Jonah 3:3; 4:11) as a great and populous city, the flourishing capital of the Assyrian empire (2 Kings 19:36; Isa. 37:37).
Nahum
(consolation). Nahum, called "the Elkoshite," is the seventh in order of the minor prophets. His personal history is quite unknown.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The justice and power of the Lord (vv. 1–8); The overthrow of the Assyrians (vv. 9–15). People named: Nahum, Elkoshite, Carmel. Places: Nineveh, Bashan, Lebanon, Judah.
ch.mh: About a hundred years before, at Jonah's preaching, the Ninevites repented, and were spared, yet, soon after, they became worse than ever.
q: Read verses 1–8 (The justice and power of the Lord). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–15 (The overthrow of the Assyrians), what do you learn about judgment?
Verse 7 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside John 10:27. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Nahum’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of suffering and endurance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Nahum?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us look forward with cheerful hope to a world where the wicked never can enter, and sin and temptation will no more be known.
ch.a: Let the seriousness of God's judgment move you to examine your ways and to pray for others.

o: The true cause, their sinning against God, and his appearing against them.
bg: nahum, book of

Nahum prophesied, according to some, in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz (B.C. 743). Others, however, think that his prophecies are to be referred to the latter half of the reign of Hezekiah (about B.C. 709).
Nineveh

About B.C. 633 the Assyrian empire began to show signs of weakness, and Nineveh was attacked by the Medes, who subsequently, about B.C. 625, being joined by the Babylonians and Susianians, again attacked it, when it fell, and was razed to the ground. The Assyrian empire then came to an end, the Medes and Babylonians dividing its provinces between them.
Huzzab

(fixed), according to the general opinion of the Jews, was the queen of Nineveh at the time when Nahum delivered his prophecy. (Nahum 2:7) (B.C. about 700.) The moderns follow the rendering in the margin of our English Bible--"that which was established."
ch.s: This chapter covers: Nineveh's destruction foretold (vv. 1–10); The true cause, their sinning against God, and his appearing against them (vv. 11–13). People named: Jacob, Huzzab. Places: Nineveh.
ch.mh: Nineveh shall not put aside this judgment; there is no counsel or strength against the Lord.
q: Read verses 1–10 (Nineveh's destruction foretold). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 11–13 (The true cause, their sinning against God, and his appearing against them), what do you learn about worship and praise?
Verse 10 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Joel 2:6. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jacob’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of war and conflict in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Nahum?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us then come to God upon his mercy-seat, that having peace with him through our Lord Jesus Christ, we may know that he is for us, and that all things shall work together for our everlasting good.
ch.a: Write down three things this chapter shows about God and thank Him for each.

o: The sins and judgments of Nineveh.
bg: nahum, book of

Nahum prophesied, according to some, in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz (B.C. 743). Others, however, think that his prophecies are to be referred to the latter half of the reign of Hezekiah (about B.C. 709).
Nineveh

First mentioned in Gen. 10:11, which is rendered in the Revised Version, "He [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria and builded Nineveh." It is not again noticed till the days of Jonah, when it is described (Jonah 3:3; 4:11) as a great and populous city, the flourishing capital of the Assyrian empire (2 Kings 19:36; Isa. 37:37).
No

Or No-A'mon, the home of Amon, the name of Thebes, the ancient capital of what is called the Middle Empire, in Upper or Southern Egypt. "The multitude of No" (Jer. 46:25) is more correctly rendered, as in the Revised Version, "Amon of No", i.e., No, where Jupiter Amon had his temple.
Ethiopia
Ethiopia is spoken of in prophecy (Ps. 68:31; 87:4; Isa. 45:14; Ezek. 30:4-9; Dan. 11:43; Nah. 3:8-10; Hab. 3:7; Zeph. 2:12).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The sins and judgments of Nineveh (vv. 1–7); Its utter destruction (vv. 8–19). People named: Ethiopia. Places: Nineveh, No, Egypt, Assyria.
ch.mh: When proud sinners are brought down, others should learn not to lift themselves up.
q: Read verses 1–7 (The sins and judgments of Nineveh). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–19 (Its utter destruction), what do you learn about war and conflict?
Verse 5 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Jeremiah 13:26. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Ethiopia’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of leadership and kingship in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Nahum?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.a: Show the same mercy you have received to someone who does not deserve it.
